articles.title: Iran-backed militias tortured him, but Iraqi environmentalist refuses to quit
articles.summary: Iran-backed militias kidnapped and tortured him, but Iraqi environmentalist is still on a mission to save marshes, and a way of life stretching back to the dawn of history.
body: CENTRAL MARSHES, southern Iraq — For all he's been through, environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi still approaches each sighting of wildlife in Iraq's marshes as if it's the very first time — even though he has seen them thousands of times before.
"Do you see?" he asks excitedly, pointing out a white egret perched on the back of a water buffalo as his long, narrow boat glides by. "It's a buffalo! With a bird on its back!"
Kingfishers with bright flashes of blue on their wings perch on reeds rising up from the shallow water. A wild boar and her piglets dart in front of the boat and disappear into the tangled grass.

Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes, monitoring water levels and talking to fishermen and buffalo herders to find out what difference a season of rain has made in the biggest wetlands in the Middle East.

Five devastating years of drought dried out some of the marshlands. In places where water remained, it was brackish, stunting the reeds and grass. Water buffalo were dying from lack of food and contaminated water.
Residents who make their living from breeding the animals and selling milk and cream headed with their remaining herds in search of water or to the outskirts of southern Iraqi cities.

They have now begun to return, repopulating some of the tiny floating islands where, aside from some modern technology, marsh residents live a way of life little changed since Sumerian times, more than 4,000 years ago.

Asadi is a leading environmental figure in Iraq. In the 1990s, in retribution for a Shiite uprising in southern Iraq, Saddam Hussein drained the marshes and set parts of them on fire to flush out resistance fighters.

After Saddam was toppled in the U.S.-led invasion in 2003, Asadi and Iraqi-American environmentalist Azzam Alwash helped residents tear down packed earth embankments holding back water from the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and the water flooded back in.
The two engineers founded the environmental organization Nature Iraq in 2004.

Asadi has been a high-profile figure, working with embassies and government ministries to garner support for the marshes and helping successfully lobby for inclusion as a UNESCO world heritage site in 2016. The inscription recognized the marshlands' biodiversity and their legacy as the site of one of the world's oldest civilizations.
Gregarious, welcoming and with a zeal for showcasing his homeland, Asadi frequently took Western journalists through the marshes, often hosting them at the Nature Iraq offices.
Kidnapped, tortured and accused of working for Israel

In February 2023, Asadi was kidnapped by an Iran-backed Iraqi militia, which accused him and the journalists he met of being Israeli spies who had fomented anti-government protests that had rocked Iran a few months earlier.

He was returning from Baghdad to his southern hometown of Chibayish after a meeting with the Iraqi president to discuss help for destitute families in the marshes when gunmen in pickup trucks and SUVs cut off his car on the road south.
They blindfolded him and threw him onto the floor of a vehicle, and with their feet on top of him drove him to what he believed to be farmland. There he was beaten and told to confess to being a spy.

"They showed me a map of the world," he says. "They were showing it on a screen and there were networks on it, connecting all the countries of the world — in Europe, Africa, Asia, America — to Tel Aviv. They said 'You are not just a spy, you lead a spy network from all the capitals of the world to Israel.'"

They accused him of ferrying journalists, whom they also accused of being spies, across the marshes into Iran. Nature Iraq, like almost all non-governmental organizations, often takes journalists and others on tours in Iraq to raise environmental awareness.
Asadi, who is 69 now, was born in the marshes — literally in a boat when his mother went into labor two months early while she was collecting reeds and grass.
"When I opened my eyes the first time, I opened my eyes to the blue sky, to the water, to the reeds and also birds," he says. "My mom returned home with the grasses, reeds and a baby."

At the age of 6 he rowed his own small boat to school. In the rainy season he says, the students would collect reeds to put on the classroom floors and when the school flooded there would be fish swimming under their desks.
In 1978, he was jailed for nine months for refusing to sign allegiance to Saddam Hussein's Baath party.
Asadi says when he was kidnapped three years ago and refused to admit to being a spy after being beaten, his captors decided he should be tortured.
They held him for two weeks. Asadi says they placed a plastic bag over his head until he thought he would suffocate and plunged his head underwater over and over.
"When the oxygen ran out I felt like I was going to die," he says.
They ran electric shocks through his body.

"They started from my feet, to my head, my genitals, my chest, my nose," he says in his office in Chibayish, on the edge of the central marshes. "They suspended him from the ceiling "like a sheep being slaughtered."

"They took my left arm behind my neck, and my right arm next to it, and beat them with metal chains. You feel like you're being pulled apart," he says. "I would scream, I would be on the verge of fainting, then they would stop and say, "So will you admit it?""
Then they would throw him back into his cell to await the next torture session.
He says the waiting was also a form of torture.
"You think about your family, you think about your children and you think of your fate in the coming days and your fate in the coming sessions."
Asadi is also a poet. He wrote his first poem when he was 13 and has memorized many hundreds of other Arab poets' writings.

"I found a way to recite poetry to myself, so I didn't have to think about anything but poetry," he says. "When I hear the sound of the cell door opening — it means they are coming to take me, they are going to torture me."
Even now, in the boat three years later, he recites poems to himself — over several minutes — start to finish.

The one he told himself hundreds of times in captivity is called In Those Days, by Saadi Youssef, an Iraqi poet from the southern port city of Basra jailed in Iraq decades ago before he went into exile in Algeria and the U.K.

"I left the court with the guards' beatings and the judge's ridicule," reads part of the poem in translation. "I have a wife whom I love and a book made of date palms." Asadi recites it in Arabic like a mantra. It comforted him, he says, to imagine that he himself was the prisoner in Youssef's poem decades ago.

After two weeks, his masked captors, dressed in military uniforms and using phrases that Asadi said were uniquely Iranian, told him he could either sign a confession that he ran spy networks and smuggled journalists into Iran, or he could write a will.
They placed a pen and a piece of paper in front of him and gave him an hour. If he didn't confess, they said, "We are going to kill you today."

"So I wrote my will," Asadi says. "I wrote that I love Iraq very much. That I have not done anything wrong, not to Iraq, not to anyone else. And I said that I wish for our country to be independent and strong and at the same time I am against all hatred and division."
He asked his wife not to be too upset.
"And I wished for my children to follow in my footsteps and in my path," he says he wrote.
"Yes, though that path led to my death, we only have one life so let us live that life honorably."
Instead of killing him, his captors ended up throwing him onto the floor of a vehicle and leaving him by the side of a road in Baghdad near where his family had been told to wait for him.

Asadi, injured and weak, insisted on returning home to the marshlands the very next day. There, hundreds of marsh residents walked for miles to welcome him back, many waving celebratory posters and Iraqi flags.

Asadi says he knows the militia that kidnapped him and he believes the government did as well while he was being held. His cousin, who was driving, had memorized the license plate number of the kidnappers.
"Within two hours they found who owns the car and the name and who he works for," says Alwash, the Nature Iraq co-founder.

The Iraqi government had pledged to secure his release. But in certain areas, some of the Iran-backed militias that flourished in the security vacuum and the subsequent civil war after the U.S. invasion have grown more powerful than Iraqi security forces. And in some parts of Iraq, tribes are even more powerful still.
In the end it was Asadi's powerful Bani Asad tribe that won his release after mobilizing hundreds of armed tribal fighters to drive home their demand that he be freed.

"Four hundred members of the Asadi clan — all with guns. They surround the guy's house and say 'Ok, if he dies, you're dead'," says Alwash. "Jassim was known — I mean everybody was like, 'What the hell? Why mess around with Jassim?'"

As part of the deal for his release, Asadi says he did not pursue the case in court. He says it never occurred to him he was in danger of being kidnapped because Nature Iraq is purely environmental and not affiliated with any political party.

He was offered asylum in Europe after he was freed. He refused, saying it was what his captors wanted — for him to leave the country and stop his work. Instead he asked for asylum for two of his children, who are now in Sweden.
"He basically told people, 'Take my children away so I can work for the marshes without putting them in danger,'" says Alwash. A third child lives in the United States.
Alwash, speaking to NPR in Amman, was told by intelligence services of three different countries after Asadi was seized that he was also at risk of being kidnapped and has not returned to Iraq since.
"Iran's operating theory is that we are a Mossad operation," Alwash says of Nature Iraq. "They cannot understand why Western governments would give money to the environment."

He says Iran's suspicions about the organization go back to 2016, when Nature Iraq began a project with Iranian conservationists working on the endangered and elusive Persian Leopard in the mountains between Iran and Iraq. Two years later Iran arrested nine Iranian conservationists related to the project, accusing them of espionage.
The Iranian-Canadian co-founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation died in detention while the rest spent years in prison.

Nature Iraq has raised a generation of environmentalists working mainly from southern Iraq and Iraq's Kurdistan region. In the marshlands, the group has built floating islands for water buffalo breeders and reed guest houses intended for tourists. They have lobbied the Iraqi and regional governments to implement water policies that would revive the marshes — primarily Turkey whose huge dams have reduced the water flow downstream.

Because there is no water treatment plant, the organization has constructed a pond to naturally clean marsh water contaminated by sewage pumped from towns into the marshes. The collection pond is now full of reeds that naturally remove toxins from the water before it is pumped back out.

They are a small fraction of the cost of water treatment plants but they are still waiting for the Iraqi government to make a decision on constructing two more ponds needed near Chibayish, Asadi says.
At its peak, the environmental organization had 94 people on staff, operating in Iraq and the Iraqi Kurdistan region.

articles.title: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better
articles.summary: The two largest emitters of greenhouse gases are China and the United States. Now, the countries' stories are diverging: many Chinese provinces are reducing coal use, while the U.S. is falling behind on climate technologies.
body: As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.
For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.
"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."

But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.

This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.

The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.
" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.
Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.

China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.
Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.
"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."

The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.
"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.
These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.

Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.

While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.

Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.
The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.

Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."

This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.
"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."
A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.
Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."

Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.
Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.
"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

articles.title: Iran launches third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
articles.summary: Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the Gulf island kingdom after a roughly two-month lull in fighting.
body: CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain, its third attack in recent days on American military targets in the tiny island kingdom in the Persian Gulf after a roughly two-month lull in fighting.
After issuing an alert about the incoming fire, Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks."
The U.S. military said there was no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
The attacks have brought condemnations from the region, while analysts say that Tehran's growing economic pressures and stalled peace negotiations are raising the risk of renewed escalation.

Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.

U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.

Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.

Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.

"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."

With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.

Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.

"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has also continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas.

On Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said that a tanker was reportedly attacked twice north of Oman, and that the second strike caused a fire on board. It also received a report that a cargo vessel off the coast of Yemen repelled an attempt by armed men in a skiff to board it.

Iran's Fars news agency reported that two ships were struck by mines in the strait, causing them to catch fire. It wasn't immediately clear whether one was the incident reported by the British military's UKMTO.

In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route, which connects the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, after a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government retreated over the weekend in a setback to the anti-Houthi coalition.

articles.title: Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia
articles.summary: Trump says he plans to discuss Ukraine during his Asia trip, which contradicts what the White House previously announced. And, Silicon Valley leaders are pushing for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening, just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.

President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley, prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.

Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027. Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. Clancy's defense argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative.

Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip
articles.summary: Manila is President Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
body: MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.

The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.

As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.

Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.

First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.

The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.

Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.

"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.

Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.

But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.

When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.

Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

articles.title: Russia downs over 1,400 Ukrainian drones as Kyiv hits a key bridge in Crimea
articles.summary: Ukraine's forces targeted a key rail and road bridge between Russia and the Crimean Peninsula for a second day. Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv.
body: Russian air defenses downed more than 1,400 Ukrainian drones during a second straight night of massive attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday, as Ukraine's forces targeted a key rail and road bridge between Russia and the Crimean Peninsula for a second day.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.

The apparent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.

On Monday, Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war. On Tuesday, Russia said that it downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones.

Also Monday, Ukraine targeted the huge Kerch Bridge, a crucial span for moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea that is also a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014. Officials said that the damage then was insignificant.

But unconfirmed media reports said that Tuesday's repeat attack on the bridge severely damaged one of its two arches. The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify reports that a span of the bridge collapsed.

The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people "to refrain from trips in the direction of the bridge." He didn't mention any damage.

articles.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
articles.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.
body: Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025

Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.

The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.

Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.

Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
The suspected Chinese spy balloon was shot down days after it was spotted over the US
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.

"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.

China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.

One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

articles.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as firm reports bumper results
articles.summary: The AI chip giant reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday after the dramatic exit of Jensen Huang.
body: Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress
Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this."
The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

articles.title: Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" supporting theories online that recent disruptions affecting Microsoft, banks and flights are connected.
body: Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one another

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.

Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.
Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.

Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.
Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.
He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.

"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.
Technology-related disruptions have happened almost daily since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.

The next day, the US Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the US for more than four hours with a rare national ground stop. It was the longest halting of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US.
The US transport secretary said the issue was technical and caused by a copper wire upgrade and outdated equipment.
On Monday, a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted service at the biggest and most utilised banks in the US.
Both United and Chase said a software issue was behind the glitch.
Apple users were impacted by outages affecting iCloud and Apple Pay on Tuesday. The company said the cause was not a cyber-attack but the outage was triggered by an an internal update.
The same day, a highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications also went offline for a period of time.
Passengers wait to check in at Los Angeles International Airport as flights resume after being grounded for several hours on November 13 due to a major communications outage.
Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.
Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages.
"There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC.

"There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."
Beevers said AI is only part of the story.
"It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said.

"Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."

Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

articles.title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
articles.summary: Confirmation of Mary Peltola's victory caps of the party's rout of the Republicans in the midterms Senate election.
body: Mary Peltola defeated the state's Republican incumbent after a controversial race
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.
The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.
It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.
It is the ninth Senate seat the Democrats have taken from Republicans in the midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.
Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate, and is the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008.

Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's US Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.
Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.
Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
Could Alaska's fishing industry tilt Washington's balance of power?

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times, external reported that her team worked with people who tried to recruit so-called spoiler candidates in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.

The alleged scheme led to a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan - a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan - contesting the race.
After legal challenges, state courts ruled that Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.

Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the US justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.
The Trump administration also filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.
A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.
Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could have simply chosen both men, listing them as their first and second choices.
If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would have re-allocated any votes from Daniel J Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to Dan S Sullivan.
Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.
An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for Daniel J Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, Peltola would still have won.
The Democratic win in Alaska cements the party's majority in the US Senate, as the party now has 56 seats to the Republicans' 44.

The most senior Democrat in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, said Peltola had run "a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about". Hailing the Democrats' final tally in the Senate, he said: "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago."

The Alaska seat was initially one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the US Senate. But by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50% of the votes, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.
Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.
"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

articles.title: Crimean Bridge badly damaged as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.summary: Zelensky says the attack took weeks to plan, while the Kremlin vows to rebuild the strategic bridge.
body: Images circulated on social media appeared to show part of the road section of the Crimea bridge has collapsed
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.
A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing.
The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the Crimea bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the Crimea bridge strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This strike could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to china.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage, and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
The Crimea bridge (pictured in 2023) has been repeatedly targeted by Ukraine - one of the two distinctive white arches appears to have collapsed overnight
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
These latest Russian strikes will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
The Northern Bridge (pictured in October) is closed after being targeted again by Russia
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

articles.title: Thomas Markle charged over child sex abuse material in Philippines
articles.summary: Markle is being held in custody in the US after one charge and has previously denied all of the allegations.
body: Thomas Markle has also been charged in the US
Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC.

Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

articles.title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
articles.summary: Moscow has targeted bridges in Kyiv, while Ukraine severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
body: Masha was in her kitchen when she heard the explosions blast through the city
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.

The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
The Northern Bridge crossing is closed to traffic while emergency response teams work to clear the debris
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.

A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.

The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
The main bridges over the River Dnipro - that cuts through Kyiv - were the target of Russian strikes
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.

Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.

The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"What else could I do?" she shrugged.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

articles.title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
articles.summary: Palestinians say there was an attack by settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, while the Israeli military says the settlers fired after being attacked.
body: A funeral was held for Fadda al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Tuesday

A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.

There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.

According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
All settlements are illegal under international law.
Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday evening

Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.

According to Palestinian accounts, her son rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said.

The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
The IDF said that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.
Doctors at a hospital in Jericho said that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.

The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.
Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.
A group of settlers set up a new outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo)

In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.

The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.

Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".
The UK government said on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.
